paperInfo.subject: Agric, Science & Tech
paperInfo.paperName: Grade 7 Agric, Science & Tech — Paper 2 (Structured Bank)

questions.questionText:
A farmer notices that the topsoil is being washed away after heavy rain.
- (a) Name the process taking place. [1 mark]
- (b) State two causes of the problem. [2 marks]
- (c) Give two methods of controlling it. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Process taking place:** **Soil erosion** (specifically sheet/raindrop-splash water erosion stripping fertile upper topsoil across bare slopes) [1 mark]. **(b) Two causes of the problem:** heavy torrential rainfall striking exposed, bare unmulched soil directly, plus poor land practices such as **overgrazing, deforestation, or ploughing straight up and down slopes** rather than across contours [2 marks]. **(c) Two methods of controlling it:** building graded **contour ridges / contour ploughing** across the slope to intercept runoff, and applying **organic grass mulch or planting cover grass/vetiver strips** to shield topsoil and bind crumbs with roots [2 marks].

Soil erosion destroys farm productivity fastest because topsoil—holding nearly all dark organic humus, beneficial earthworms, nitrogen, and water-absorbing crumbs—lies only in the top 15–20 cm above sterile subsoil or bedrock. Once naked soil loses vegetation cover, pounding raindrops break soil aggregates apart, sealing surface pores so rainwater rushes swiftly down tracks and carves shallow sheet wash into deep unstoppable gullies.

In ZIMSEC Grade 7 Agriculture & Science Paper 2, do not merely name *"trees"* vaguely when asked for control methods—state actionable techniques cleanly (**ploughing along the contour**, **mulching bare inter-rows**, **terracing**, **planting vetiver grass strips**, or **rotational grazing**).

questions.questionText:
A school starts a compost heap using crop residues and kitchen waste.
- (a) Define compost. [1 mark]
- (b) State two materials that can be composted. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why water is added during compost making. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of compost:** Well-decomposed, dark, crumbly **organic fertiliser** formed naturally when plant residues, dry grass, kitchen vegetable wastes, and small amounts of manure rot down steadily under controlled moisture and air [1 mark]. **(b) Two compostable materials:** dry maize stalks/grass (*carbon-rich "brown" matter*) paired with green vegetable peelings, weeds before flowering, or kraal/poultry manure (*nitrogen-rich "green" activators*) [2 marks]. **(c) Why water is added:** Essential moisture activates and sustains **decomposer micro-organisms (beneficial bacteria and fungi)** inside the heap so they multiply rapidly, digest tough plant fibres into rich humus, and regulate healthy fermentation warmth [2 marks].

A properly layered compost heap relies on living microscopic decomposers that work just like tiny soil farmers: if the heap turns bone-dry, bacteria stop breaking stems down completely, whereas soaking it soggy drowns oxygen air pockets and turns the pile smelly and anaerobic! Sprinkling water gently like a **wrung-out damp sponge** and turning every 3–4 weeks balances air, warmth (~55–65°C inside), and moisture smoothly.

Examiners check specifically that you state **living micro-organisms / bacteria / fungi need moisture to survive and break down the waste**, and remind farmers never to toss **meat scraps, cooking oil, glass, plastics, or thick diseased twigs** onto garden compost heaps.

questions.questionText:
A farmer grows maize and keeps cattle on the same farm.
- (a) Name the type of farming enterprise involving both crops and livestock. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two benefits of integrating crops and livestock. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how manure can support crop production. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Type of farming enterprise:** **Mixed farming** (raising crops and domesticated farm livestock together in one integrated farm unit) [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of integrating crops and livestock:** spreading household financial and drought **risk across multiple income sources** (selling milk or goats if maize prices dip), plus building a **self-feeding biological cycle** where dried maize stover, sorghum stalks, and garden trimmings become cheap winter cattle feed while cattle/goat manure enriches crop fields [2 marks]. **(c) How manure supports crop production:** cured livestock manure returns essential plant macronutrients (**nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium**) and trace minerals while adding spongy **organic humus** that loosens heavy clay, thickens light sandy water storage, and boosts harvest yields [2 marks].

Smallholder mixed farms in Zimbabwe remain far more resilient than pure monocrop farms because cattle pull ox-ploughs for timely planting in November, provide fresh milk daily, and convert tough inedible crop stalks into dark soil-building manure without buying expensive imported bags every season.

Keep distinct **Mixed Farming** (both crops and livestock deliberately integrated on the same farm) versus **Monoculture** (repeatedly growing one single crop species across fields season after season).

questions.questionText:
A farmer plans to irrigate vegetables during a dry period.
- (a) Name one irrigation method. [1 mark]
- (b) State two advantages of irrigation. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain one risk of poor irrigation management. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named irrigation method:** **Drip irrigation** (delivering slow water drops cleanly straight to each plant root), **sprinkler irrigation**, or **furrow/basin irrigation** [1 mark]. **(b) Two advantages of irrigation:** frees farmers from total reliance on unpredictable rains by permitting **year-round winter and off-season cropping**, and protects tall yields reliably against destructive mid-season dry spells [2 marks]. **(c) One risk of poor irrigation management:** **over-irrigating poorly drained soils** causes **waterlogging** (driving life-giving oxygen out of root air spaces so roots suffocate and rot), **leaches soluble nitrogen fertilisers** below active roots, and spreads fungal soil diseases [2 marks].

Comparing methods smartly matters too: **drip irrigation** saves up to 50% more scarce borehole water than overhead sprinklers during windy afternoons because drops soak directly at shaded plant bases without evaporating mid-air or wetting foliage with fungal spores.

Always match the irrigation fault to its exact consequence in Paper 2: **too much water → waterlogging + root oxygen starvation + nutrient leaching**; **using salty/dirty water → soil salinisation or crop contamination**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer keeps dairy cattle.
- (a) What is dairy farming? [1 mark]
- (b) State two requirements for healthy dairy cattle. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why clean water is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of dairy farming:** Keeping specialised cattle breeds (such as **Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, or Mashona/crossbred dairy cows**) primarily for clean, high-volume **milk production** and dairy products [1 mark]. **(b) Two requirements for healthy dairy cattle:** supplying abundant **balanced, high-protein/energy rations** (lush pasture/napier fodder plus dairy meal concentrates) alongside **clean, shaded, mud-free housing, gentle hygiene at milking, and routine dipping/vaccinations** [2 marks]. **(c) Importance of clean water:** fresh milk is **~87% water**, so lactating cows must drink huge daily volumes (**50–90+ litres per cow daily**) of clean fresh water to synthesise milk cleanly, cool body heat, digest rough dry hay, and prevent waterborne scours or mastitis contamination [2 marks].

Even a top-pedigree Holstein cow eating expensive dairy concentrates drops litres sharply within 24 hours if troughs run empty or sit slimy and stagnant—water is literally the single highest-volume nutrient in a milk bucket!

In ZIMSEC answers on dairy nutrition, quoting that **milk is roughly 85–87% water** makes your biological reason immediately airtight and earns full marks effortlessly.

questions.questionText:
A crop is attacked by insects.
- (a) Define a pest. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two methods of pest control. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why integrated pest management can be useful. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of a pest:** Any living organism—including biting/sucking **insects, mites, nematodes, rodents (rats), grain-eating birds, competing weeds, or disease fungi**—that damages crops, feeds on stored harvests, or lowers agricultural yield and quality [1 mark]. **(b) Two pest-control methods:** targeted **chemical control** (applying safe approved insecticides/fungicides cleanly) alongside **biological control** (encouraging natural predators like ladybirds eating aphids) or **cultural rotation and hand-picking** [2 marks]. **(c) Value of Integrated Pest Management (IPM):** combining preventive cultural sanitation, mechanical traps, biological predators, and sparing last-resort chemicals slashes spraying **costs**, prevents pests from evolving **chemical resistance**, protects friendly **honeybees/pollinators**, and reduces toxic food residues [2 marks].

Think of IPM as defending a fortress in layers: resistant crop seeds and clean weeded edges stop pests from settling first, natural predators guard plants daily, and careful targeted sprays step in only when pest counts cross real economic danger levels.

Never define pests narrowly as *"bad bugs"* only—remember ZIMSEC includes **insects, rodents, weeds, birds, and pathogens** as crop pests whenever they harm agricultural productivity.

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to improve soil fertility.
- (a) Name one organic manure. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits of organic manure. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one precaution when handling manure. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Named organic manure:** **Kraal (cattle/goat) manure, poultry droppings, or garden compost** [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of organic manure:** rebuilds dark spongy **organic humus** that loosens sticky clay and boosts moisture retention in dry sand, while steadily feeding crops with slow-release balanced macronutrients and trace minerals at almost zero cash cost [2 marks]. **(c) Precaution when handling manure:** ensure fresh raw manure (especially hot concentrated chicken droppings!) is **properly rotted/cured** before touching tender vegetable seedlings so soluble ammonia does not scorch delicate roots, and **wash hands thoroughly with soap** after handling dung [1 mark].

Unlike quick mineral fertilisers that dissolve overnight and leach down fast during storms, dark cured organic manure nourishes soil earthworms and beneficial microbes that glue fine dust particles into airy water-holding soil crumbs lasting several seasons.

Notice the twin handling precautions examiners expect: **(1) curing raw dung so heat/ammonia doesn't burn young plants** AND **(2) personal soap hygiene (plus avoiding spreading raw manure onto ready-to-eat raw salad leaves!)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer stores harvested grain for several months.
- (a) State one condition required for safe grain storage. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two storage pests or problems. [2 marks]
- (c) Give two ways of reducing storage losses. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Condition for safe grain storage:** harvested maize, sorghum, or beans must first be **dried thoroughly down to low moisture (~12–12.5%)** and kept inside a **cool, dry, waterproof, well-ventilated, pest-sealed granary or store** [1 mark]. **(b) Two storage pests/problems:** destructive boring insects like **maize weevils (*Sitophilus*) and Larger Grain Borer (*Prostephanus*)**, **rodents/rats**, and toxic **storage moulds** (*Aspergillus* producing poisons) [2 marks]. **(c) Two ways to reduce storage losses:** storing spotless dry grain inside **airtight hermetic bags (e.g. PICS bags) or sealed metal silos** that suffocate insects without poison, or cleaning/dusting empty granaries cleanly, sealing rat-gaps, and applying approved grain protectant dusts on bags stacked on raised **wooden pallets** [2 marks].

Smallholder farmers often lose up to a third of hard-won grain between May and December solely from rushing slightly damp cobs into old dusty cribs—simply testing dryness cleanly ("teeth bite crack test" or salt-jar check) saves whole sacks from rotting silently.

Include both **physical/structural protection (dry ≤ 12% moisture, pallets off damp floors, clean stores)** and **pest exclusion (hermetic bags, safe grain protectants, rat traps/guards)**.

questions.questionText:
A herd of cattle is grazing continuously in one small area.
- (a) Name the problem that may result. [1 mark]
- (b) State two effects of overgrazing. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest two grazing-management measures. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Problem resulting:** **Overgrazing** (stocking too many grazing animals continuously onto one small paddock faster than pasture grass can regrow reserves) [1 mark]. **(b) Two effects of overgrazing:** sweet nutritious grass species get bitten down to bare roots and die out (replaced by tough unpalatable thorn scrub), leaving bare compacted trampled earth swept swiftly into **severe sheet and gully soil erosion** during summer storms [2 marks]. **(c) Two grazing-management measures:** dividing pastures into fenced **rotational grazing paddocks** so each grazed block enjoys long recovery rest while stock graze fresh blocks, and balancing herd size cleanly to the land’s **carrying capacity** (supplementing winter herds with hay/stover instead of starving veld bare) [2 marks].

Grass plants store energy in underground roots: continuous close nibbling every day drains root reserves completely so plants starve, whereas letting grass rest after short grazing turns paddocks thicker and deeper-rooted every rainy season.

Link **continuous grazing on one small area → overgrazing → loss of palatable grasses + exposed compacted soil → erosion**, and give concrete fixes (**rotational grazing paddocks**, **matching carrying capacity**).

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to reduce livestock disease.
- (a) Name one disease-prevention measure. [1 mark]
- (b) State two hygiene practices. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain the value of vaccination. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named disease-prevention measure:** **Timely vaccination, routine tick dipping/spraying, or strict quarantine of new/sick stock** [1 mark]. **(b) Two hygiene practices:** regularly sweeping, scrubbing, and **disinfecting livestock kraals, pens, and footbaths**, alongside supplying spotless **clean feeding troughs and fresh drinkers** free of manure droppings [2 marks]. **(c) Value of vaccination:** vaccines introduce safe harmless/weakened germs into healthy animals **before** outbreaks strike, stimulating the animal’s immune system to produce protective **antibodies** against deadly killers like **Newcastle Disease, Anthrax, or Blackleg** [2 marks].

Remember that vaccination works strictly as a *shield for healthy animals*—waiting until half the fowl run is dying to buy vaccines wastes money because antibodies take 10–14 days to build up safely.

Keep sharp clarity between **Vaccination (builds preventive immunity in healthy animals beforehand)** versus **Antibiotics (treats bacterial infections only after sickness strikes)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer uses a knapsack sprayer.
- (a) State one use of a knapsack sprayer. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two safety precautions. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why chemical labels must be followed. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Use of a knapsack sprayer:** **Applying carefully diluted liquid pesticides (insecticides/fungicides), weed-killing herbicides, or liquid foliar fertilisers** evenly over crops [1 mark]. **(b) Two safety precautions:** wearing full **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)** (impermeable gloves, face mask/respirator, goggles, overalls, and gumboots) and **never spraying into facing wind** (nor eating, drinking, or smoking while handling chemicals) [2 marks]. **(c) Why chemical labels must be followed:** labels state exact safe **mixing dilution rates** (avoiding poisonous residues or crop leaf scorch), specific target pests, PPE warnings, and mandatory **Pre-Harvest Intervals (PHIs)** telling farmers how many days to wait safely before picking food [2 marks].

Spraying early morning or late calm evening protects beneficial honeybees (which forage during sunny midday hours) while ensuring fine chemical droplets settle neatly onto leaves rather than blowing straight back into the farmer’s eyes.

Never give thin advice like *"be careful"*—state concrete **PPE items (mask, gloves, goggles, boots)**, **wind direction rule**, and exact **label reasons (dilution + Pre-Harvest Interval + poisoning avoidance)**.

questions.questionText:
A farm manager keeps records of sales, inputs and expenses.
- (a) Name the management practice. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits of farm records. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how records help decision-making. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Management practice:** **Farm record keeping** (maintaining written/digital physical production and financial transaction books systematically) [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of farm records:** proves accurately whether each enterprise earned a **net profit or cash loss**, while tracking daily **feed/fertiliser usage, animal vaccinations, calving dates, and missing tools/theft** [2 marks]. **(c) How records help decision-making:** comparing past seasonal records spotlights the highest-earning enterprises vs money-losing crops, supports realistic **next-season budgets**, spots pest/disease timings early, and provides solid proof banks inspect before approving **agricultural credit loans** [2 marks].

Memory tricks every farmer into remembering peak harvests while forgetting dozens of small mid-season cash leaks—written ledgers make quiet small expenses visible on one page.

Separate clearly **production records** (yields, rainfall, mortalities) from **financial records** (receipts, costs, profit), and highlight **budgeting + enterprise comparison + bank loans**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to reduce financial risk.
- (a) Define risk in farming. [1 mark]
- (b) State two ways of reducing risk. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain the value of diversification. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Risk in farming:** **Unpredictable uncertain hazards**—such as sudden drought, hailstorms, armyworm outbreaks, foot-and-mouth disease, or sharp market price drops—that can ruin yields or cause serious financial loss [1 mark]. **(b) Two ways of reducing risk:** spreading production across **enterprise diversification**, buying **agricultural crop/livestock insurance**, or investing in **irrigation and staggered planting dates** [2 marks]. **(c) Value of diversification:** raising several independent enterprises together (for instance **maize + sugar beans + goats + broilers**) means that if drought hits maize or tomato market prices crash, steady goat and egg cash still buys family food and covers farm debts [2 marks].

"Never put all your eggs in one basket" holds especially true under rainfed Zimbabwean skies: mixing hardy drought-tolerant small grains with deep-rooted crops and hardy indigenous livestock shields homesteads against single-event shocks.

Differentiate clearly between **avoiding risk before planting (diversification, irrigation, drought-hardy varieties)** and **transferring financial loss (insurance, savings reserves)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer selects healthy seeds before planting.
- (a) State one characteristic of good seed. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two reasons for using good seed. [2 marks]
- (c) State one condition needed for germination. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Characteristic of good seed:** **High germination percentage (>85–90%)**, plumb clean unwrinkled size, pure true-to-variety identity, and **complete freedom from weevil holes, rot, weed seeds, and seed-borne disease spores** [1 mark]. **(b) Two reasons for using good seed:** delivers **fast uniform vigorous seedling emergence** capturing early rains and shading weeds out cleanly (raising final yield), while preventing farmers from accidentally planting dangerous **parasitic weed seeds or blight germs** into fresh soil [2 marks]. **(c) Condition needed for germination:** sufficient **water/moisture** to soften seed coats and activate enzymes, paired with adequate **warmth** and **oxygen air** for seed respiration [1 mark].

Testing saved or bought seed a month early by wrapping 20 seeds inside a damp cloth/paper towel for 7 days reveals true **germination %** cheaply—saving farmers from wasting basal fertiliser beneath dead seed!

Never write *"sunlight"* as one of the three classic germination conditions in Grade 7 science/agriculture—almost all crop seeds germinate underground in total darkness given **Water + Oxygen + Suitable Warmth**!

questions.questionText:
A farmer uses crop rotation.
- (a) Define crop rotation. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how rotation can help manage pests or fertility. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of crop rotation:** Growing **different crop families in a planned, recurring seasonal sequence** across divided farm plots rather than planting the same crop repeatedly on one patch [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits:** disrupts specialist **soil pests and plant diseases**, balances extraction of **mineral nutrients at varied rooting depths**, and suppresses host-specific weeds like witchweed (*Striga*) [2 marks]. **(c) How rotation helps pests or fertility:** including **legumes** (groundnuts, cowpeas, beans) allows *Rhizobium* bacteria in root nodules to **fix free atmospheric nitrogen** into fertile nitrates for demanding maize next year, while switching botanical families starves specialist root nematodes and blights between host seasons [2 marks].

Remember that a genuine rotation rotates **botanical plant families** cleanly—e.g. **Cereal (Maize) → Legume (Beans) → Root/Leaf (Sweet Potato/Cabbages)**—because planting tomatoes straight after potatoes fails to break blight or nematode cycles!

Score maximum marks by explicitly naming **Rhizobium nitrogen fixation in legume root nodules** AND **breaking host-specific soil pest/disease cycles**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to protect a stream beside a field.
- (a) Name one source of agricultural water pollution. [1 mark]
- (b) State two ways of protecting the stream. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why water conservation is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Source of agricultural water pollution:** surface storm runoff washing excess **mineral fertilisers, sprayed agrochemicals (pesticides/herbicides), livestock dung slurry, or eroded mud silt** from bare fields into the stream [1 mark]. **(b) Two ways to protect the stream:** strictly preserving an **uncultivated 30-metre green riverbank buffer zone** (streambank grass/trees filtering silt and chemicals) and **fencing livestock out while piping clean water to cattle troughs** away from stream banks (plus washing sprayers far away from water!) [2 marks]. **(c) Why water conservation matters:** clean fresh water is a scarce, finite survival resource essential year-round for **safe family drinking, garden irrigation, livestock health, and living river fish/ecosystems** [2 marks].

Zimbabwe’s Environmental Management Act protects 30-metre stream margins specifically because ploughing right down to river edges lets eroded mud choke dams while manure and nitrate leaks poison community boreholes and choke rivers with algae (*eutrophication*).

Connect pollution sources (**fertiliser nutrients, toxic pesticides, animal manure, eroded mud**) straight to proven farm shields (**30 m riparian vegetation buffer + fenced off-stream cattle troughs + careful chemical mixing sites**).

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates why some plants grow faster than others.
- (a) Name one factor affecting plant growth. [1 mark]
- (b) State two environmental requirements of plants. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain the role of light in photosynthesis. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Factor affecting plant growth:** **soil nutrient fertility, water moisture supply, sunlight brightness/duration, temperature warmth, or weed/pest pressure** [1 mark]. **(b) Two environmental requirements of plants:** balanced soil **water and dissolved mineral salts** taken in via roots, plus atmospheric **carbon dioxide** and radiant **sunlight energy** captured by leaves [2 marks]. **(c) Role of light in photosynthesis:** green **chlorophyll** pigments inside leaf chloroplasts absorb **sunlight energy** and use that light power to chemically combine **carbon dioxide and water into glucose (plant sugar/energy)** while releasing oxygen gas [2 marks].

Whenever plants sit crowded under dense tall tree shade, pale yellowing thin stems stretch desperately toward light (*etiolation*) yet stay weak because low photon energy starves photosynthesis—proving sunlight is literally the energy battery running plant food factories!

Write **chlorophyll absorbs light energy to drive the conversion of carbon dioxide + water into glucose** clearly rather than vaguely saying *"light helps leaves look green"*.

questions.questionText:
A learner observes a leaf under suitable conditions.
- (a) Name the process by which green plants make food. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two materials required. [2 marks]
- (c) State one product of the process. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Process:** **Photosynthesis** (how green plants manufacture organic food energy using sunlight) [1 mark]. **(b) Two raw materials required:** **carbon dioxide** (entering leaves from air through tiny pores called **stomata**) and **water** (absorbed up from moist soil via root hairs and xylem vessels), powered by **sunlight** and **chlorophyll** [2 marks]. **(c) One product formed:** **glucose** (soluble sugar stored later as starch for stems, roots, and grain!) along with life-giving **oxygen gas** released into air [1 mark].

Without green plant photosynthesis turning solar energy and air into edible sugars and fresh breathable oxygen, neither grazing cattle nor human beings could survive on Earth—making green plants the foundational **producers** in every ecosystem!

Examiners expect clear distinction between the two true raw chemical **inputs** (**Carbon Dioxide + Water**) vs the **conditions** enabling the reaction (**Sunlight + Chlorophyll**) vs the **outputs** (**Glucose + Oxygen**).

questions.questionText:
A learner measures the temperature of water before and after heating.
- (a) Name the instrument used. [1 mark]
- (b) State one safety precaution. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain what happens to particles as water is heated. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Instrument used:** **Thermometer** (liquid-in-glass laboratory/clinical thermometer or digital temperature probe, calibrated in degrees Celsius **°C**) [1 mark]. **(b) One safety precaution:** handle hot beakers carefully with **tongs or heatproof gloves**, keep glass thermometers off bare burner bottoms using gentle stirring, and keep faces away from rising steam [1 mark]. **(c) Particle behaviour when heated:** heating transfers thermal energy into liquid water molecules, raising their **kinetic energy** so particles **vibrate and move faster, collide harder, and spread slightly farther apart** until fast surface molecules escape into steam/vapour at boiling point (**100°C** at sea level) [2 marks].

Understanding rising kinetic particle energy explains why hot water rises inside solar geysers, expands inside sealed kettles, and evaporates off damp soil far faster on hot afternoons than on chilly mornings!

Always use exact scientific particle-model keywords in Paper 2: **gain kinetic energy → move faster → overcome attractions/spread apart**—never write *"particles melt or grow bigger"*.

questions.questionText:
A simple electric circuit contains a cell, wires, a switch and a lamp.
- (a) Name the energy source. [1 mark]
- (b) State the condition needed for the lamp to light. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain the function of the switch. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Energy source:** The **electric cell (or battery)**, which converts stored **chemical energy** into **electrical energy** pushing charge through the circuit [1 mark]. **(b) Condition needed for the lamp to light:** the circuit must form an unbroken **complete closed conducting loop** connecting cell terminals cleanly through good copper wires, switch, and intact lamp filament without flat dead batteries or loose breaks [1 mark]. **(c) Function of the switch:** acts as an intentional safe **bridge/break in the conducting circuit**—closing the switch completes the loop so electric current flows lighting the lamp, while opening the switch breaks the path safely stopping current flow and conserving cell energy [2 marks].

If a bulb fails to light in class, tracing loop continuity methodically—checking fresh cell contact, tight wire screws, intact fine tungsten bulb filament, and closed metal switch contacts—pinpoints faults rapidly!

Use accurate Grade 7 electricity language: **complete closed loop** (not *"round wire"*), **chemical-to-electrical energy transfer inside the cell**, and **switch controls opening/closing the conducting path**.

questions.questionText:
A learner compares transparent, translucent and opaque materials.
- (a) Define transparent. [1 mark]
- (b) Give one example of an opaque material. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain how shadows form. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of transparent:** A material that allows **nearly all incident light rays to pass straight through clearly without scattering**, enabling objects behind it to be seen sharply—for example **clear window glass, clean still water, or clear perspex** [1 mark]. **(b) One opaque material:** **wood, brick wall, solid sheet metal, cardboard, or stone** (blocks all light completely) [1 mark]. **(c) How shadows form:** because light rays travel strictly in **straight lines** (rectilinear propagation) and cannot bend round solid barriers, placing an **opaque object** in front of a light source blocks rays straight ahead, creating a **dark unlit region (shadow)** directly behind it on a screen or ground [3 marks].

By contrast, *translucent* materials like frosted bathroom glass or greased paper let partial light through while scattering rays sideways so shapes appear blurred!

Always state the fundamental physical law clearly in shadow questions: **Light travels in straight lines**, so an **opaque object blocks rays** cleanly behind it.

questions.questionText:
A family wants to reduce electricity use.
- (a) State two ways of saving electricity. [2 marks]
- (b) Name one renewable energy source. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain one advantage of renewable energy. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two ways to save electricity at home:** strictly **switching off lights, geysers, and appliances when rooms sit empty**, and replacing old hot incandescent filaments with high-efficiency **LED bulbs**, solar water heaters (*geyser timers*), or cold-water laundry cycles [2 marks]. **(b) One renewable energy source:** **solar (sunlight) photovoltaic energy, hydroelectricity (falling water), wind turbine power, or biogas** [1 mark]. **(c) Advantage of renewable energy:** renewable sources are **naturally replenished endlessly without running dry** (unlike finite coal or diesel!) and generate clean electricity with **little or no harmful carbon greenhouse gas emissions or choking air smoke** [2 marks].

Across sunny Zimbabwean schools and homesteads, rooftop solar panels powering boreholes and LED lights simultaneously lower monthly ZESA bills while keeping lighting dependable during grid load-shedding!

Pair concrete household efficiency actions cleanly with exact definitions—knowing **renewable = naturally replenished cleanly (solar/hydro/wind)** versus **non-renewable = finite fossil fuels (coal/petrol)**.

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates friction by moving objects over different surfaces.
- (a) Define friction. [1 mark]
- (b) State one useful effect. [1 mark]
- (c) State one harmful effect. [1 mark]
- (d) Explain how surface texture affects friction. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of friction:** A **contact force acting along touching surfaces that opposes sliding or rolling motion** between two objects moving (or trying to move) across each other [1 mark]. **(b) Useful effect:** rough friction grips shoe soles safely on floors for **walking without slipping**, lets **bicycle/car brakes slow tyres**, and holds knots/nails tightly [1 mark]. **(c) Harmful effect:** unwanted rubbing wears away **tractor tyres, gear teeth, and hinges**, slows moving bicycles down, and wastes useful kinetic energy as **unwanted frictional heat** [1 mark]. **(d) How surface texture affects friction:** microscopic bumps and ridges on **rough surfaces** (gravel, sandpaper) interlock deeply creating **very high friction**, whereas **smooth polished or oiled/greased surfaces** glide past with far lower interlocking resistance [2 marks].

Notice farmers rely on *both* sides daily: deep tyre treads raise traction friction in muddy fields, while smooth grease inside wheelbarrow bearings cuts harmful wear!

Remember friction is a **force opposing relative motion between touching surfaces**, increased by **roughness & heavy weight** and reduced by **smoothness, oil/grease lubrication, or ball bearings**.

questions.questionText:
A learner studies a food chain in a grassland.
- (a) Name the producer. [1 mark]
- (b) Name one consumer. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain the direction of energy transfer. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) The producer:** **Grass (or green plants)**—organisms capturing sunlight energy via photosynthesis to build food for every link above them [1 mark]. **(b) Named consumer:** **Grasshopper / zebra / impala** (*primary consumer* herbivore eating grass) or **lion / leopard** (*secondary/tertiary consumer* carnivore eating herbivores) [1 mark]. **(c) Direction of energy transfer:** energy flows **in one single direction** starting from the **Sun → Producers (grass) → Primary Consumers (herbivores) → Secondary/Tertiary Consumers (carnivores)**—arrows point strictly toward the eater, and large amounts of usable energy are lost as **warmth/heat during respiration and movement** at every step [2 marks].

Because roughly ~90% of captured energy exits as body heat or waste between trophic steps, natural savannas support vast fields of grass, smaller herds of zebras/impala, and relatively few top lions!

Check your arrows in food-chain diagrams: arrows NEVER point from lion back to zebra—arrows always show **direction energy flows (from food organism → consumer)**.

questions.questionText:
A pond becomes polluted with waste.
- (a) Name one pollutant. [1 mark]
- (b) State two effects on organisms. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest two ways to reduce the pollution. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named water pollutant:** **raw untreated sewage, agricultural fertiliser runoff, toxic pesticides, plastic litter, or waste engine oil** [1 mark]. **(b) Two effects on aquatic organisms:** excess sewage/fertiliser runoff triggers thick surface **algal blooms** that decay and strip out **dissolved oxygen**, **suffocating fish and water insects**, while oil coats bird feathers/gills and toxic chemicals poison frogs and spread human **cholera/bilharzia** [2 marks]. **(c) Two ways to reduce water pollution:** enforce proper **waste-bin disposal/recycling** and **sewage treatment works** away from streams, alongside maintaining unploughed **vegetated riverbank buffer strips** and fixing leaking factory/tractor oil sumps [2 marks].

Clean aquatic ecosystems filter community drinking supplies naturally and supply nutritious bream/kapenta protein when farms and towns keep plastics, sewage, and toxic sprays strictly out of storm drains!

Don't stop at saying *"pollution kills fish"*—name *why* (**oxygen depletion / eutrophication**, **direct chemical toxicity**, or **clogging plastic/oil**) for full Paper 2 credit.

questions.questionText:
A learner studies the human digestive system.
- (a) Name the organ where digestion begins. [1 mark]
- (b) State one function of the stomach. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why the small intestine is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Organ where digestion begins:** **The mouth**—where teeth grind food mechanically (**mastication**) into small moist pieces while saliva’s **amylase** enzyme begins breaking starch into simple sugars chemically [1 mark]. **(b) Function of the stomach:** muscular stomach walls churn swallowed food smoothly with **hydrochloric acid** (killing swallowed germs!) and protease **pepsin enzymes** to initiate **protein breakdown** into semi-liquid chyme [1 mark]. **(c) Importance of the small intestine:** serves as both the final site of **complete chemical digestion** (breaking carbohydrates, proteins, and fats completely into soluble molecules) and the main site of **nutrient absorption** through millions of finger-like **villi** straight into the bloodstream [2 marks].

After useful nutrients cross tiny thin villi walls into blood capillaries feeding body cells, undigested roughage moves into the *large intestine* where vital water is absorbed back before egestion!

Distinguish cleanly between **Mouth (chewing + salivary starch digestion)**, **Stomach (acid germ-killing + protein digestion)**, **Small Intestine (final digestion + villi nutrient absorption)**, and **Large Intestine (water absorption)**.

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates disease prevention.
- (a) Name one communicable disease. [1 mark]
- (b) State two ways of reducing transmission. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why handwashing is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named communicable disease:** **Cholera, malaria, tuberculosis (TB), measles, typhoid, or influenza**—infectious sicknesses capable of passing directly or via vectors from person to person [1 mark]. **(b) Two transmission-reduction measures:** consistent **handwashing with clean water and soap** alongside **safe pit/flush sanitation**, childhood **immunisations**, sleeping under insecticide-treated **mosquito nets** (for malaria), or wearing masks/covering coughs cleanly [2 marks]. **(c) Why handwashing matters:** soap and running water lift and wash away invisible **bacteria and viruses** picked up on fingers after using toilets, touching shared surfaces, or handling dirty soil—stopping dangerous pathogens from entering mouths when eating or preparing family meals [2 marks].

Breaking transmission chains works far cheaper than hospitalising whole villages during rainy-season cholera outbreaks: boiling questionable borehole/well water cleanly alongside rigorous soap handwashing stops waterborne outbreaks cold!

Notice you should pair **correct disease category** (**communicable/infectious** vs non-communicable like diabetes/kwashiorkor!) with **matching prevention routes** cleanly.

questions.questionText:
A learner observes day and night.
- (a) Name the movement responsible for day and night. [1 mark]
- (b) State the approximate time Earth takes to complete one rotation. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why different places experience different times of day. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Earth movement causing day and night:** **Rotation of the Earth spinning around its own tilted North-South axis** (spinning eastward from west to east) [1 mark]. **(b) Time for one complete rotation:** **24 hours** (defining one full Earth solar day) [1 mark]. **(c) Why different places have different times:** because Earth is a curved sphere, as it spins smoothly only the **hemisphere facing the Sun experiences bright daylight** while the opposite dark side experiences **night**—causing eastern longitudes (e.g., Tokyo/Harare ahead of London/New York) to receive sunrise earlier across global **time zones** [2 marks].

Keep careful distinction between Earth’s **Rotation** on its axis (**24 hours → Day and Night**) versus Earth’s longer **Revolution** orbiting around the Sun (**365¼ days → Annual Calendar Seasons**)!

One of the classic Grade 7 Paper 2 traps is swapping **rotation** and **revolution**—lock down **"Rotation = 24 hours = Day & Night"** vs **"Revolution = 365 days = Year & Seasons"**.

questions.questionText:
A class investigates water changing state.
- (a) Name the change from liquid to gas. [1 mark]
- (b) Name the change from gas to liquid. [1 mark]
- (c) Give one example of each change in everyday life. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Liquid to gas change:** **Evaporation** (slow surface escape into invisible vapour at any warm temperature) or rapid bubbling **Boiling** throughout the liquid at 100°C [1 mark]. **(b) Gas to liquid change:** **Condensation** (warm invisible water vapour cooling down when striking cold surfaces to form tiny liquid water droplets) [1 mark]. **(c) One everyday example of each:** **Evaporation**—wet washed school uniforms drying cleanly on an outdoor clothes line under breeze and sunshine (or puddles drying off tarmac); **Condensation**—shiny liquid water droplets beading outside an ice-cold drink bottle, inside a boiling pot lid, or forming morning dew and rain clouds high in chilly sky [2 marks].

Both evaporation and condensation drive Earth’s continuous **Water Cycle**: solar heating evaporates dam and ocean water skyward, while high cold air condenses rising vapour back into visible clouds that return precious rain onto fields!

Be precise in terminology: avoid calling vapour *"steam"* loosely in physics—explain **liquid absorbs heat to evaporate** while **gas loses heat (cools) to condense** back into liquid drops.

questions.questionText:
A learner uses a microscope to observe a specimen.
- (a) State the purpose of a microscope. [1 mark]
- (b) Give one rule for handling it safely. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why very small structures can be studied with it. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Purpose of a microscope:** a precision optical instrument designed to **magnify (enlarge) invisible microscopic structures**—such as plant onion cells, blood cells, bacteria, or tiny leaf stomata—hundreds of times larger than naked human eyes can resolve [1 mark]. **(b) Safe handling rule:** always carry the microscope upright with **two steady hands** (one gripping the curved **arm**, one supporting safely beneath the heavy **base**), keep lenses clean strictly with soft **lens tissue**, and start focusing cautiously upward so glass slides never crack against lenses [1 mark]. **(c) How tiny structures become clear:** carefully curved glass **objective and eyepiece lenses refract (bend) incoming light beams** sequentially, multiplying magnification (e.g. 10× eyepiece × 40× objective = 400× enlargement) to show crisp internal organelles cleanly [2 marks].

Remember that if you ever draw magnified biology specimens in exams, you compute exact enlargement using **Magnification = Image Size ÷ Actual Size** (*M = I ÷ A*)!

Always check two practical lab habits: **two-handed carry (arm + base)** AND **focussing carefully upward using coarse knob on low power first** to avoid crushing precious glass slides.

questions.questionText:
A class tests a hypothesis by changing one factor at a time.
- (a) Define hypothesis. [1 mark]
- (b) Why should other relevant conditions be controlled? [2 marks]
- (c) State one way of recording results. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Definition of hypothesis:** A clear, **testable scientific prediction or educated explanation** stated *before* testing an experiment—for instance predicting *"Bean seedlings watered every two days will grow taller than unwatered seedlings"* [1 mark]. **(b) Why control other relevant conditions:** keeping all extra factors identical (**soil type, light exposure, seed variety, pot size, and temperature**) creates a genuine **fair test** so the scientist proves confidently that ONLY the single factor intentionally changed (**independent variable**) caused the observed difference [2 marks]. **(c) Way of recording results:** neat **labelled data tables**, **bar charts or line graphs**, and dated **observation measurement logs** showing units like millimetres or grams cleanly [1 mark].

Without holding irrelevant variables constant—imagine putting watered beans in sunny windows while hiding unwatered beans inside dark cupboards!—nobody could tell whether extra height came from water or sunlight!

Make the **fair-test rule** crystal clear in Paper 2: change **only ONE independent variable**, measure the **dependent outcome**, and hold **every control variable equal**.

questions.questionText:
A learner finds that an iron nail rusts faster in a wet place.
- (a) Name the change taking place. [1 mark]
- (b) State two conditions that encourage rusting. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest one method of preventing rust. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Chemical change taking place:** **Rusting**—a slow irreversible chemical **oxidation** reaction converting shiny iron/steel into flaky reddish-brown iron oxide [1 mark]. **(b) Two conditions encouraging rusting:** presence of BOTH **water/moisture** AND **oxygen gas (from air)** touching exposed bare iron together (salty rain or damp farm mud speeds rust even faster!) [2 marks]. **(c) One method of preventing rust:** creating a barrier sealing air and water away from metal by **painting** gates/ox-ploughs, wiping moving parts with **oil or grease**, **galvanising** roof sheets in protective **zinc**, or storing tools strictly inside dry sheds [1 mark].

If you seal an iron nail completely inside boiled water topped with an oil layer (no oxygen!) OR inside a dry sealed jar with drying calcium chloride (no water!), the nail stays bright silver for months—proving **both oxygen and water** are simultaneously mandatory!

Rusting attacks **iron and steel specifically** (aluminium or plastic does not rust!), so list barrier protections clearly (**paint, oil/grease, zinc galvanising, dry storage**).

questions.questionText:
A learner studies magnets.
- (a) Name one material attracted by a magnet. [1 mark]
- (b) What happens when like poles are brought together? [1 mark]
- (c) State one use of magnets. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** **(a) Material attracted by a magnet:** **Iron, steel, nickel, or cobalt** (magnetic metals—not copper wire, brass, plastic, glass, or aluminium cans!) [1 mark]. **(b) Like poles brought together:** **like poles REPEL each other forcefully**—North pushes away North (*N–N*), and South pushes away South (*S–S*), whereas opposite poles (*N–S*) attract [1 mark]. **(c) Use of magnets:** guiding direction inside **magnetic compasses**, holding **fridge door seals shut**, driving electric **motors/loudspeakers/dynamos**, or separating scrap iron cans cleanly at recycling depots [1 mark].

A classic Grade 7 trap tests magnetic vs non-magnetic metals: even though **copper coins, gold rings, and aluminium pots** are shiny metals, **NONE of them stick to magnets**—only **Iron, Steel, Cobalt, and Nickel** are attracted!

Memorise the golden magnetism rhyme: **"Like poles repel, unlike poles attract"**—and remember **repulsion**, not attraction, is the surest test proving a metal bar is truly a magnet (since plain iron attracts too!).

questions.questionText:
A family wants to reduce household waste.
- (a) Define recycling. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two materials that can be recycled. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain one environmental benefit. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of recycling:** Collecting used discarded waste items (that might otherwise fill dumpsites or rivers) and **reprocessing them industrially or creatively into useful brand-new products** [1 mark]. **(b) Two recyclable materials:** **clear plastic PET bottles, aluminium drinks cans, scrap iron/copper, clean waste paper/cardboard boxes, and glass jars/bottles** [2 marks]. **(c) One environmental benefit:** drastically **cuts unsightly plastic/landfill pollution**, saves finite natural **mineral ores and forest trees**, and consumes far less electricity/coal burning than smelting new aluminium or paper from raw earth [2 marks].

Notice how recycling fits inside the famous **"3 Rs" environmental waste hierarchy** right alongside **Reduce** (buying fewer wasteful single-use plastics) and **Reuse** (refilling sturdy glass jars or tote bags many times before discarding)!

Show clear contrast in Paper 2: **Reusing** washes an existing bottle cleanly to hold seeds/water again unchanged, whereas **Recycling** melts/pulps waste material physically into new manufactured items.

questions.questionText:
A school uses computers for research and presentations.
- (a) Name one input device. [1 mark]
- (b) Name one output device. [1 mark]
- (c) State one benefit of ICT in learning. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Named computer input device:** **Keyboard, mouse, scanner, touchscreen, microphone, or webcam** (sending user commands/data *into* the computer) [1 mark]. **(b) Named output device:** **Monitor screen, laser/inkjet printer, speakers, or classroom data projector** (displaying processed results *out* to learners) [1 mark]. **(c) Benefit of ICT in learning:** expands access to **interactive educational textbooks, animated science simulations, word-processed neat assignments, spreadsheet calculations, and fast academic research** connecting rural or urban classrooms cleanly to current knowledge [2 marks].

Understanding the simple data pipeline (**Input → CPU Processing → Storage & Output**) helps learners troubleshoot cables immediately when microphones stay muted or projectors show no image!

Keep **Input (keyboard/mouse/scanner)** and **Output (monitor/printer/speakers)** strictly separate—never call a *flash drive/USB* an input/output device unless noting it is **storage media**!

questions.questionText:
A learner creates a password for an online account.
- (a) State two characteristics of a strong password. [2 marks]
- (b) Give one reason passwords should remain private. [1 mark]
- (c) State one action to take if an account is compromised. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Two traits of a strong password:** at least **8–12+ unique characters long** combining **uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, and special symbols** (e.g. *!@#*) while strictly avoiding easy personal guesses like names, "123456", birthdays, or phone numbers [2 marks]. **(b) Why keep passwords private:** prevents cyber-thieves, bullies, or unauthorised strangers from opening private accounts, **stealing identity/school files, deleting projects, or sending harmful messages pretending to be you** [1 mark]. **(c) Urgent action if compromised:** **immediately reset/change the password** on that account (and any matching accounts!), turn on **Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)**, log out active strange devices, and inform a trusted **parent, teacher, or school IT administrator** [1 mark].

Using unique memorable passphrases (mixing unrelated words plus numbers/symbols!) keeps accounts easy for learners to remember while blocking automatic password-guessing tools.

Include exact **character variety + length (8–12+ mixed characters)** rather than writing simply *"make it hard"*, and name **changing password + enabling 2FA + alerting an adult/IT admin**.

questions.questionText:
A class stores learner information in a database.
- (a) What is a database? [1 mark]
- (b) What is a record? [1 mark]
- (c) State two benefits of organising information in a database. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Definition of a database:** An **organised, structured electronic collection of related information** stored cleanly inside tables so facts can be searched, filtered, sorted, and updated rapidly by computer [1 mark]. **(b) What is a record:** One complete **horizontal row** containing all linked details (fields) describing **one single person, book, or farm item**—such as a single learner’s Student ID, Full Name, Grade, Birthdate, and Guardian Phone together [1 mark]. **(c) Two benefits of electronic databases:** delivers **lightning-fast searching and alphabetical/numeric sorting** across thousands of entries in seconds, while sharply cutting **bulky paper file clutter, duplicate mistakes, and lost sheets** when properly backed up [2 marks].

Think of a neat school attendance ledger: the entire ledger is the **Table/Database**, each column (*Surname, Age, Grade*) is a **Field**, and every single learner’s line straight across is one **Record**!

Examiners love seeing the clear structural hierarchy: **Character/Data → Field (column) → Record (one full row) → Table → Database**.

questions.questionText:
A learner prepares a presentation for a science project.
- (a) Name one presentation application. [1 mark]
- (b) State two features that can make a presentation clear. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one rule for responsible use of images or information. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Presentation application:** **Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, or LibreOffice Impress** [1 mark]. **(b) Two features making slides clear:** using concise **short readable bullet points** (never crammed full textbook paragraphs!) paired with **large high-contrast clean fonts** and well-labelled **diagrams, charts, or sharp photos** illustrating key science concepts [2 marks]. **(c) Responsible citation rule:** never steal classmates’ or online creators’ photos and text silently—always **credit the original author/website source neatly** and use **copyright-free, Creative Commons, or teacher-permitted resources** [1 mark].

Remember the presentation golden rule: slides exist to *visualise* key highlights cleanly for the audience sitting in the back row while the presenter speaks smoothly—never turn slides into tiny walls of text read word-for-word off the screen!

Combine **visual design clarity** (short bullets + high contrast + clean fonts/diagrams) cleanly with **digital citizenship (citing sources & respecting copyright)**.

questions.questionText:
Two learners communicate using an internet-based voice call.
- (a) Name the technology generally associated with internet voice calls. [1 mark]
- (b) State one advantage. [1 mark]
- (c) Give one safety or privacy precaution. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** **(a) Internet voice technology:** **VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol)**—carrying live human voice/video packets cleanly across internet connections (such as WhatsApp audio/video calls, Zoom, Google Meet, or Teams) [1 mark]. **(b) One advantage:** enables **much cheaper real-time long-distance communication** across cities or countries using internet data instead of pricey international phone minutes, and easily allows **multi-person group study calls with screen sharing** [1 mark]. **(c) Safety/privacy precaution:** answer calls **strictly from known verified contacts** (classmates/teachers/family), hold private meetings using passcodes/waiting rooms, and **never reveal private passwords, home addresses, or financial PINs** aloud or on camera [1 mark].

Using clean headphones in quiet rooms with strong stable Wi-Fi prevents echoing feedback and keeps distant learner study collaborations clear and focused.

Write out what **VoIP** actually stands for (**Voice over Internet Protocol**) and connect internet calls clearly to **cost savings + group learning** plus **contact verification / privacy rules**.

questions.questionText:
A school computer has been infected by malicious software.
- (a) Name the general term for such malicious software. [1 mark]
- (b) Name one tool used to help detect it. [1 mark]
- (c) Give two safe computing practices. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) General term for malicious software:** **Malware** (encompassing harmful **computer viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, and ransomware** designed to damage files or steal private data) [1 mark]. **(b) Detection & removal tool:** Up-to-date **Antivirus / Anti-malware security software** configured for regular full-drive scans [1 mark]. **(c) Two safe computing practices:** always **scan external USB flash drives** before opening files, **never click suspicious unknown links or weird email attachments**, download apps solely from trusted official stores, and keep **operating systems + antivirus signatures updated** [2 marks].

Notice how just one infected student USB flash drive plugged casually into a computer lab PC without scanning can infect twenty classroom machines before lunch break—making careful **USB hygiene** every learner’s daily shield!

Always distinguish the umbrella term **Malware** cleanly (instead of thinking "virus" covers nothing else), name **Antivirus software**, and cite **USB scanning + avoiding suspicious links/attachments**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer plants different crops in successive seasons.
- (a) Name the practice. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two benefits. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how it may affect soil fertility. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Farming practice:** **Crop rotation** (growing distinct crop families in a planned recurring order across farm plots) [1 mark]. **(b) Two agricultural benefits:** sustains higher stable yields per hectare cleanly and breaks persistent **host-specific crop pests, soil nematodes, fungal blights, and parasitic weeds** (like *Striga*) by depriving them of consecutive host plants [2 marks]. **(c) Effect on soil fertility:** alternating **shallow-rooted heavy feeders (maize/covo)** with **deep-rooted taproot/tuber crops** extracts soil minerals evenly across different root depths, while rotating in **legumes (beans, groundnuts, cowpeas)** adds fresh fixed soil **nitrogen** naturally via *Rhizobium* root-nodule bacteria [2 marks].

Unlike relentless maize-after-maize monocropping that mines topsoil bare and explodes stalk-borer numbers every November, a tidy 4-year Cereal → Legume → Root → Rest/Manured rotation keeps soil crumbly, darker, and productive year after year.

Always tie rotation’s fertility power cleanly to **two clear mechanisms**: **(1) Legume Rhizobium bacteria adding nitrogen** AND **(2) Varying root depths utilising topsoil & subsoil minerals evenly**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer uses a windbreak around a field.
- (a) What is a windbreak? [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how it can reduce soil erosion. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of windbreak:** A dense **barrier belt of tall hardy trees or tall perennial shrubs** planted cleanly across the windward edge of fields, orchards, or gardens to intercept strong prevailing winds [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits:** dramatically protects tall crops (like maize, bananas, and tomatoes) from **physical stem snapping and wind lodging**, and lowers harsh dry surface winds—reducing **evaporation water loss from soil and excessive plant leaf transpiration** [2 marks]. **(c) How it reduces soil erosion:** slowing tearing wind speed close down at ground level strips gusts of their lifting energy so fine dry dusty **topsoil grains and organic ash cannot be picked up and blown away** (*wind erosion*) during dry August–October months [2 marks].

Ideal farm windbreaks avoid dense solid stone walls (which swirl damaging eddies right behind!)—instead mixing tall feathery trees (*Grevillea*, *Casuarina*, citrus/mango belts, or tough Napier grass hedges) letting gentle filtered air pass softly at slower calm speeds.

Include both **physical crop damage protection (preventing lodging/wilting)** AND the exact **erosion physics (slowing wind velocity near ground stops dust lifting/wind erosion)**.

questions.questionText:
A poultry farmer keeps laying birds.
- (a) Name one suitable housing requirement. [1 mark]
- (b) State two management practices. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why clean nesting areas are useful. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Suitable layer housing requirement:** A **clean, dry, well-ventilated, draught-free and predator-proof poultry house** stocked with dry absorbent floor **deep litter**, sturdy **perches**, and quiet darkened **laying nest boxes** [1 mark]. **(b) Two essential management practices:** supplying balanced **layers mash** alongside continuous **clean fresh drinking water** daily, while collecting eggs **3–4 times every day**, cleaning feeders, and following **Newcastle/Gumboro vaccination schedules** [2 marks]. **(c) Why clean nesting boxes matter:** soft, clean, dry straw/shavings inside quiet raised nest boxes stop hens from laying directly on soiled floor droppings—dramatically preventing **manure-stained dirty shells, cracked broken eggs, bacterial yolk rot, and sneaky egg-eating habits** so eggs earn top Grade A retail prices [2 marks].

Supplying roughly **one clean nest box per 4 to 5 laying hens** positioned in shaded calm corners prevents birds from crowding and breaking freshly laid warm eggs underfoot!

Cover **housing safety/ventilation + perches/nests**, **layers nutrition + frequent collection/vaccines**, and **exact egg-quality protection (cleanliness + zero cracks + stopping egg-eating)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer keeps bees for honey.
- (a) Name the enterprise. [1 mark]
- (b) State two products obtained. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one importance to crop pollination. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Farming enterprise:** **Apiculture** (the scientific keeping and management of **honeybee colonies** inside wooden hives for honey and pollination) [1 mark]. **(b) Two hive products obtained:** pure sweet nutritious **honey** and natural **beeswax** (used for candles, shoe polish, cosmetics, and soap—plus valuable **propolis** and **royal jelly**) [2 marks]. **(c) Importance to crop pollination:** as honeybees visit bright blossoms gathering nectar and pollen, hairy bee legs carry pollen dust smoothly between flowers (**cross-pollination**), dramatically lifting fruit set, plumpness, and **seed yields in sunflowers, citrus orchards, avocados, pumpkins, cucumbers, and beans** [1 mark].

Placing clean modern *Kenya Top-Bar* or *Langstroth* hives safely inside shaded quiet boundary woodlots (well away from cattle kraals and pesticide sprays!) generates lucrative cash honey while quietly multiplying surrounding orchard harvests!

Make sure you spell **Apiculture (bees)** accurately—do NOT confuse it with *Aquaculture* (fish farming)!—and state clearly **cross-pollination increases fruit and seed yield**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer keeps fish in a managed pond.
- (a) Name the enterprise. [1 mark]
- (b) State two pond-management requirements. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why water quality matters. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Farming enterprise:** **Aquaculture** (controlled rearing and harvesting of aquatic fish like **tilapia/bream (*Oreochromis*) or catfish** in managed ponds, cages, or tanks) [1 mark]. **(b) Two pond-management requirements:** maintaining steady watertight **clay/lined pond depth** with screened overflow pipes, applying balanced floating **fish pellets or organic pond fertilisation** (promoting natural green plankton algae), protecting stock beneath **bird/predator netting**, and keeping gentle water flow/aeration [2 marks]. **(c) Why water quality matters:** fish breathe **dissolved oxygen directly through gills** inside that water all day—cloudy muddy sediment clogs delicate gills, rotting excess leftover feed strips oxygen out and builds lethal **ammonia poison**, causing slow growth, gill infections, or sudden mass **fish suffocation kills** [2 marks].

Watch pond colour gently as a natural gauge: healthy fertile tilapia ponds look a clean light **emerald/pea-green tint** rich in natural plankton food rather than murky brown mud or stinking black scum!

Pair **Aquaculture (fish)** clearly against *Apiculture (bees)*, and explain **dissolved oxygen for gill respiration + preventing toxic ammonia/disease** directly.

questions.questionText:
A learner investigates how exercise affects breathing.
- (a) Name the body system involved. [1 mark]
- (b) Describe one change during exercise. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why the change occurs. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Body system involved:** The **Respiratory system** (supported closely by lungs, trachea, diaphragm, and chest ribs working alongside the circulatory system) [1 mark]. **(b) Change observed during exercise:** both **breathing rate** (breaths taken per minute) and **depth of each breath** (tidal air volume inhaled) **increase markedly** [1 mark]. **(c) Why the change occurs:** actively contracting leg and arm muscles perform faster **cellular respiration** to release extra ATP energy—demanding urgent increased **oxygen intake** while generating extra waste **carbon dioxide** that faster deeper breathing rapidly expels from lungs [2 marks].

Right alongside faster breathing, your **heart beats faster** too so blood shuttles freshly oxygenated red blood cells quickly out to hungry working muscles while carrying waste carbon dioxide straight back to lungs!

Mention BOTH measurable breathing changes (**faster rate AND deeper volume**) AND BOTH gas reasons (**bringing MORE oxygen in + removing MORE waste carbon dioxide out faster**).

questions.questionText:
A learner observes that a plant wilts after several hot days.
- (a) State one possible cause. [1 mark]
- (b) Explain the role of water in plants. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one method of reducing water loss. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Possible cause of wilting:** severe **soil water shortage** after dry days, or intense midday heat forcing leaves to lose water faster through **transpiration** than roots can absorb water upward [1 mark]. **(b) Role of water in plants:** water fills internal plant vacuoles pressing firmly against cell walls to keep soft stems upright and leaves **turgid** (preventing wilting!), carries **dissolved soil minerals** upward through xylem tubes, cools hot leaves, and acts as an essential chemical **raw material for photosynthesis** [2 marks]. **(c) Method to reduce plant water loss:** spreading clean **organic mulch** across root soil (cutting surface evaporation), watering during cool dawn/dusk hours, removing competing thirsty weeds, or temporarily shading vulnerable transplants [1 mark].

Notice that if a farmer notices wilting only at 2:00 p.m. on scorching sunny afternoons when wet soil actually sits moist below, temporary shading eases leaf transpiration—whereas morning wilting signals urgent deep watering before permanent wilt damage kills roots!

Keep key Grade 7 biology vocabulary sharp: **turgor / turgidity** keeps non-woody plants standing crisp upright, while **transpiration** drives water loss from tiny underside leaf **stomata**.

questions.questionText:
A learner separates a mixture of iron filings and sand.
- (a) Name the method. [1 mark]
- (b) Explain why it works. [2 marks]
- (c) Name another separation method used for a different mixture. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Separation method:** **Magnetic separation** (sweeping a strong bar/horseshoe magnet cleanly across or just above the dry mixture) [1 mark]. **(b) Why this method works:** separation exploits a sharp physical property difference—tiny **iron filings are strongly magnetic** and jump straight onto magnet poles cleanly, whereas dry **sand grains (silica) are non-magnetic** and stay completely untouched behind in the tray [2 marks]. **(c) Another mixture & separation method:** **Filtration** (filtering insoluble mud/sand out from murky water using filter paper and a funnel), **Evaporation** (recovering dissolved table salt crystal cleanly from salt water), or **Winnowing** (separating light chaff from heavy sorghum/maize grain in wind) [1 mark].

In clean laboratory practice, wrapping a thin clean plastic bag or paper sheet tightly round the magnet before dipping into iron filings lets you strip collected pure iron dust cleanly into a separate dish afterward!

State the exact **difference in physical properties** making every separation trick work (**magnetic vs non-magnetic** for iron+sand; **insoluble particle size** for filtration; **boiling point** for evaporation/distillation).

questions.questionText:
A learner tests whether light affects plant growth.
- (a) State a suitable hypothesis. [1 mark]
- (b) Identify the variable being changed. [1 mark]
- (c) Name two variables that should be kept constant. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Suitable testable hypothesis:** **"Green seedlings exposed to bright natural sunlight will grow taller, sturdier, and deep dark green compared with identical seedlings kept completely inside a dark cupboard"** [1 mark]. **(b) Variable intentionally changed (Independent Variable):** the **presence, brightness, or duration of light** received by the two test groups of plants [1 mark]. **(c) Two variables held strictly constant (Control Variables):** keeping identical **daily water volume measured per pot**, exact same **soil type/volume, seed variety/starting age, and surrounding air temperature** across both light and dark trays [2 marks].

Notice what fascinating biology shows up in real school jars too: seeds kept in total darkness often shoot up pale, yellow, spindly thin stems desperately searching for light before exhausting stored seed food and collapsing, whereas sunlit seedlings stay stocky, green, and crisp with fresh chlorophyll!

Always verify experimental design alignment: **(1) Independent = what YOU deliberately change (Light)**; **(2) Dependent = what you MEASURE (height/colour)**; **(3) Controls = everything kept strictly equal**.

questions.questionText:
A learner observes a shadow at different times of day.
- (a) State what causes the shadow. [1 mark]
- (b) Describe one change in shadow length. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why the shadow changes. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Cause of the shadow:** An **opaque solid pole, learner, or tree blocking straight-travelling sunlight rays**, casting a dark silhouette behind it across the ground [1 mark]. **(b) Change observed through the day:** shadows stretch **very long westward** early after sunrise, shrink **shortest cleanly overhead near solar noon/midday**, and lengthen **steeply eastward** again late before sunset [1 mark]. **(c) Why shadow length shifts:** as **Earth rotates steadily eastward on its axis** over 24 hours, the Sun’s apparent **angle/altitude above the horizon** sweeps smoothly upward from low oblique morning rays (casting long shadows) to high overhead noon rays (casting short shadows) before dropping low again [2 marks].

Before mechanical wristwatches existed, ancient sun-clocks (**sundials**) measured working hours accurately simply by tracking how stick shadows shortened, rotated, and stretched calmly from morning to dusk!

Tie both directional shift AND length shift neatly together: **low morning/evening sun angle → LONG shadows** vs **high overhead midday sun angle → SHORT shadows**, driven by **Earth’s daily rotation**.

questions.questionText:
A school wants to protect learners' digital privacy.
- (a) State two pieces of personal information that should be protected. [2 marks]
- (b) Give two safe online practices. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Two sensitive personal details to guard:** **exact residential home street address, private account passwords/banking PINs, national ID/birth certificate numbers, and personal family phone numbers** [2 marks]. **(b) Two safe digital privacy habits:** securing accounts with strong unique private passwords (never shared even with close friends!), setting social/learning profiles strictly to **private/friends-only**, avoiding uploading uniform badges or live GPS location photos publicly, and **never sharing private info or meeting online strangers** [2 marks].

Cyber-scammers and online groomers frequently piece tiny harmless-looking clues together—like a school crest on a uniform photo plus a house number—to locate learners offline or impersonate families for money scams!

Cover both **sensitive identity/access credentials (passwords, ID numbers, home address)** AND **proactive privacy behaviours (privacy locks, refusing stranger chats, guarding location photos)** cleanly.

questions.questionText:
A learner accidentally deletes a project file.
- (a) Name one method that could help recover it. [1 mark]
- (b) Explain the value of backups. [2 marks]
- (c) State one good file-management practice. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) File recovery method:** open the desktop **Recycle Bin / Trash** immediately and click **Restore** to put the accidentally deleted file right back in its original folder (or retrieve the latest saved copy from **cloud storage / external USB backup**) [1 mark]. **(b) Value of regular backups:** maintaining separate extra copies on **cloud drives, external hard disks, or labelled USB drives** guarantees weeks of school projects, grades, or farm accounts survive even if a laptop hard drive crashes, power surges burn circuits, or ransomware locks the main computer [2 marks]. **(c) Good file-management practice:** organise work neatly inside clearly named **subject/date folders** (e.g., *Grade7_Agri_Project_2026_v2*), press **Ctrl+S** frequently while typing, and empty clutter periodically without rashly deleting master folders [1 mark].

Follow the practical **3-2-1 backup habit** for important schoolwork: keep one working copy on your computer plus one extra backup saved safely off-device on cloud drive or an external memory stick!

Note why backups matter *more* than Recycle Bin alone: **Shift+Delete** or a stolen/broken computer skips the Recycle Bin forever, whereas an off-device **backup** saves everything safely.

questions.questionText:
A learner uses a spreadsheet to record crop yields.
- (a) Name one type of data that can be entered. [1 mark]
- (b) State one benefit of formulas. [1 mark]
- (c) Explain why organised data is useful. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Types of data entered in a spreadsheet:** **Numeric figures** (kilograms harvested, hectares planted, unit prices $), **Text labels** (crop names like Maize/Beans, field names), and formatted **Dates** (planting/harvest dates) [1 mark]. **(b) Benefit of formulas (=SUM, =AVERAGE, =B2*C2):** formulas compute grand totals, averages, and profit automatically with **zero mental arithmetic errors**—and recalculate instantly the second any yield or market price changes [1 mark]. **(c) Why well-organised tables matter:** laying headings cleanly across rows and columns enables instant **sorting highest-to-lowest yields, spotting data-entry errors immediately, generating clear bar/pie charts**, and making fast data-driven farm budgets [2 marks].

Always enter pure plain numbers into numeric cells (e.g., 240, not "240 kg" typed as words inside the same number cell!)—put units cleanly inside the column header "Yield (kg)" so spreadsheet formulas add cleanly without errors!

Distinguish clearly **Labels/Text vs Pure Numbers/Values vs Dynamic Formulas starting with =** for rock-solid ICT Paper 2 answers.

questions.questionText:
A class uses a search engine for research.
- (a) State one way to improve search results. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two checks for information reliability. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why copying information without acknowledgement can be problematic. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Way to tighten web search results:** enter **specific precise keywords**, wrap exact phrases inside **quotation marks "..."**, exclude noisy words using minus signs (-ads), or restrict sites cleanly to reliable domains (site:.edu, site:.gov, ZIMSEC Grade 7) [1 mark]. **(b) Two reliability checks:** inspect **author/publisher authority and credentials** (preferring respected universities, Ministries, established encyclopaedias/textbooks over anonymous blogs), check **publication date currency**, and **cross-verify facts across two or three independent reputable sources** [2 marks]. **(c) Problem with uncredited copying:** copying paragraphs verbatim without quotation marks or proper author citation constitutes **plagiarism**—a serious breach of honesty and **copyright ethics** that prevents real personal understanding and draws strict academic penalties or zero marks [2 marks].

Always practise paraphrasing researched ideas calmly in **your own fresh words** while noting book titles, authors, or clean URLs at the bottom of your assignment!

Connect **smart search syntax (exact phrases/specific keywords)**, **fact-checking (author authority + date + cross-verification)**, and **naming Plagiarism accurately**.

questions.questionText:
A school holds an online video meeting with another school.
- (a) Name the technology. [1 mark]
- (b) State two requirements for a good call. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one online etiquette rule. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Technology used:** **Video conferencing** (two-way live digital audio and video communication conducted over internet networks using applications like Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams) [1 mark]. **(b) Two requirements for a smooth call:** a **fast, reliable broadband/Wi-Fi internet connection** alongside functional **camera webcam, clear microphone, speakers/headphones**, good front lighting, and a quiet room free of echo [2 marks]. **(c) Essential online etiquette rule:** keep your **microphone muted whenever listening** so background coughing or desk noise doesn’t interrupt speakers, dress neatly, look at the camera politely, and raise your digital hand before speaking [1 mark].

Testing audio levels five minutes early and typing concise questions calmly inside the meeting **Chat box** allows rural and urban classrooms across Zimbabwe to hold smooth joint revision lessons cleanly without shouting over feedback echoes!

Include **hardware/network essentials (broadband + camera/mic/speakers)** AND specific **digital meeting manners (muting when listening, camera framing, polite turn-taking)**.
